"title": "The properties of highly concentrated aqueous CH3COOK/Na binary electrolyte and its use in sodium-ion batteries",
"authors": "Shahid Khalid, Nicolò Pianta, Simone Bonizzoni, Piercarlo Mustarelli, Riccardo Ruffo",

"type_of_paper": "Experimental study on aqueous electrolyte properties and battery application",
"executive_summary": "This work investigates highly concentrated aqueous binary electrolytes based on potassium acetate (CH3COOK) combined with varying amounts of sodium acetate (CH3COONa), aiming to develop safe, low-cost, and environmentally friendly electrolytes for sodium-ion batteries. The authors address the limitations of conventional lithium-ion batteries, which suffer from safety issues, high cost, and reliance on thermally unstable LiPF6 salt. While aqueous electrolytes offer inherent safety and environmental benefits, they are limited by the narrow electrochemical stability window (ESW) of water (1.23 V), which can only be kinetically extended to about 1.5 V in dilute solutions. To overcome this, researchers have explored super-concentrated electrolytes, including the 'Water-in-Salt' (WISE) concept, which widens the ESW by reducing water activity through high ion concentrations. However, fluorinated salts commonly used in WISE systems, such as LiTFSI, exhibit severe toxicity and high cost, limiting their practical application. In contrast, acetate salts like CH3COOK and CH3COONa are cost-effective, highly soluble, and widely available, making them attractive alternatives. The authors prepared a series of electrolytes with constant CH3COOK concentration (20 mol kg⁻¹) and varying CH3COONa concentrations (1 to 7 mol kg⁻¹), then systematically characterized their thermal, rheological, transport, and electrochemical properties. The most concentrated solution (7N20K, i.e., 20 mol kg⁻¹ CH3COOK with 7 mol kg⁻¹ CH3COONa) emerged as the best compromise between transport properties and electrochemical stability, exhibiting a conductivity of 21.2 mS cm⁻¹ at 25°C and a stability window up to 3 V under ideal conditions. As a proof of concept, the authors demonstrated the use of this electrolyte in sodium-ion batteries using a carbon-coated LiTi2(PO4)3 (NASICON) electrode, which reversibly inserted and de-inserted Na⁺ ions at about -0.7 V vs. SHE with a first-cycle anodic capacity of 85 mAh g⁻¹, average charge efficiency of 96% at low current, and 90% capacity retention after 60 cycles. The low activation energy for charge transfer (0.12 eV) highlighted the excellent interfacial kinetics. These findings support the feasibility of designing electrode interfaces for alkaline-ion rechargeable batteries using the WISE approach, offering a promising pathway toward sustainable energy storage technologies.",

summary.title: The properties of highly concentrated aqueous CH3COOK/Na binary electrolyte and its use in sodium-ion batteries
summary.authors: Shahid Khalid, Nicolò Pianta, Simone Bonizzoni, Piercarlo Mustarelli, Riccardo Ruffo
summary.field_subfield: Electrochemistry / Materials Chemistry for Energy Storage
summary.type_of_paper: Experimental study on aqueous electrolyte properties and battery application
summary.executive_summary: This work investigates highly concentrated aqueous binary electrolytes based on potassium acetate (CH3COOK) combined with varying amounts of sodium acetate (CH3COONa), aiming to develop safe, low-cost, and environmentally friendly electrolytes for sodium-ion batteries. The authors address the limitations of conventional lithium-ion batteries, which suffer from safety issues, high cost, and reliance on thermally unstable LiPF6 salt. While aqueous electrolytes offer inherent safety and environmental benefits, they are limited by the narrow electrochemical stability window (ESW) of water (1.23 V), which can only be kinetically extended to about 1.5 V in dilute solutions. To overcome this, researchers have explored super-concentrated electrolytes, including the 'Water-in-Salt' (WISE) concept, which widens the ESW by reducing water activity through high ion concentrations. However, fluorinated salts commonly used in WISE systems, such as LiTFSI, exhibit severe toxicity and high cost, limiting their practical application. In contrast, acetate salts like CH3COOK and CH3COONa are cost-effective, highly soluble, and widely available, making them attractive alternatives. The authors prepared a series of electrolytes with constant CH3COOK concentration (20 mol kg⁻¹) and varying CH3COONa concentrations (1 to 7 mol kg⁻¹), then systematically characterized their thermal, rheological, transport, and electrochemical properties. The most concentrated solution (7N20K, i.e., 20 mol kg⁻¹ CH3COOK with 7 mol kg⁻¹ CH3COONa) emerged as the best compromise between transport properties and electrochemical stability, exhibiting a conductivity of 21.2 mS cm⁻¹ at 25°C and a stability window up to 3 V under ideal conditions. As a proof of concept, the authors demonstrated the use of this electrolyte in sodium-ion batteries using a carbon-coated LiTi2(PO4)3 (NASICON) electrode, which reversibly inserted and de-inserted Na⁺ ions at about -0.7 V vs. SHE with a first-cycle anodic capacity of 85 mAh g⁻¹, average charge efficiency of 96% at low current, and 90% capacity retention after 60 cycles. The low activation energy for charge transfer (0.12 eV) highlighted the excellent interfacial kinetics. These findings support the feasibility of designing electrode interfaces for alkaline-ion rechargeable batteries using the WISE approach, offering a promising pathway toward sustainable energy storage technologies.

claims.description: Highly concentrated aqueous acetate electrolytes offer a promising, safe, and cost-effective alternative to conventional lithium-ion batteries.
The 7N20K electrolyte exhibits optimal transport and electrochemical stability properties.
The carbon-coated NASICON electrode demonstrates excellent performance in sodium-ion batteries.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This work investigates highly concentrated aqueous binary electrolytes based on potassium acetate (CH3COOK) combined with varying amounts of sodium acetate (CH3COONa), aiming to develop safe, low-cost, and environmentally friendly electrolytes for sodium-ion batteries. The authors address the limitations of conventional lithium-ion batteries, which suffer from safety issues, high cost, and reliance on thermally unstable LiPF6 salt. While aqueous electrolytes offer inherent safety and environmental benefits, they are limited by the narrow electrochemical stability window (ESW) of water (1.23 V), which can only be kinetically extended to about 1.5 V in dilute solutions. To overcome this, researchers have explored super-concentrated electrolytes, including the 'Water-in-Salt' (WISE) concept, which widens the ESW by reducing water activity through high ion concentrations. However, fluorinated salts commonly used in WISE systems, such as LiTFSI, exhibit severe toxicity and high cost, limiting their practical application. In contrast, acetate salts like CH3COOK and CH3COONa are cost-effective, highly soluble, and widely available, making them attractive alternatives. The authors prepared a series of electrolytes with constant CH3COOK concentration (20 mol kg⁻¹) and varying CH3COONa concentrations (1 to 7 mol kg⁻¹), then systematically characterized their thermal, rheological, transport, and electrochemical properties. The most concentrated solution (7N20K, i.e., 20 mol kg⁻¹ CH3COOK with 7 mol kg⁻¹ CH3COONa) emerged as the best compromise between transport properties and electrochemical stability, exhibiting a conductivity of 21.2 mS cm⁻¹ at 25°C and a stability window up to 3 V under ideal conditions. As a proof of concept, the authors demonstrated the use of this electrolyte in sodium-ion batteries using a carbon-coated LiTi2(PO4)3 (NASICON) electrode, which reversibly inserted and de-inserted Na⁺ ions at about -0.7 V vs. SHE with a first-cycle anodic capacity of 85 mAh g⁻¹, average charge efficiency of 96% at low current, and 90% capacity retention after 60 cycles. The low activation energy for charge transfer (0.12 eV) highlighted the excellent interfacial kinetics. These findings support the feasibility of designing electrode interfaces for alkaline-ion rechargeable batteries using the WISE approach, offering a promising pathway toward sustainable energy storage technologies.

Research Context
Super-concentrated aqueous electrolytes are gaining interest for safer, cheaper batteries. Conventional lithium-ion batteries face safety and cost challenges. Organic electrolytes have low flashpoints and high viscosities. LiPF6 salt degrades in moisture, producing corrosive HF. Aqueous electrolytes are limited by water's narrow stability window. The ESW can be kinetically extended only to about 1.5 V in dilute solutions. High concentration widens the ESW by reducing water activity. Fluorinated salts enable wide ESW but raise toxicity and cost concerns. LiTFSI exhibits severe toxicity and chronic aquatic effects. Acetate salts are cost-effective, soluble, and available alternatives. NASICON materials are ideal electrodes for concentrated environments.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question concerns the physicochemical properties of binary acetate electrolytes. The authors hypothesize that adding NaAc improves electrochemical stability. The most concentrated solution is expected to balance transport and stability. The hypothesis is that 7N20K offers optimal conductivity and stability. The authors predict good performance in sodium-ion batteries. The hypothesis includes favorable interfacial kinetics. The authors expect the WISE approach to enable alkaline-ion batteries.

Methodological Details
The study used high-purity acetate salts from Alfa Aesar. Milli-Q water with defined resistivity was used as solvent. Four electrolytes were prepared with varying NaAc concentrations. The compositions ranged from 1 to 7 mol kg⁻¹ NaAc. A 1 M NaAc solution was prepared for comparison. All electrolytes were stored and used at room conditions. The samples are listed in Table 1 with compositional parameters. CLTP was synthesized via a one-pot sol-gel route. Ammonium dihydrogen phosphate was used as the phosphate precursor. Titanium butoxide served as the titanium source. Lithium acetate dihydrate and glucose were used as Li and C sources. The mixture was stirred at 55°C for 4 hours. The temperature was raised to 80°C to form a gel. The precursor was dried under vacuum at 100°C. Calcination was performed at 800°C for 6 hours under argon. The ramp rate was set to 5°C per minute. The gas flow was adjusted to 50 ml per minute. Pristine LTP was synthesized without glucose. XRD analysis used a Rigaku Miniflex 600 with Cu cathode. The XRD range was 10 to 80 degrees with a step size of 0.02. SEM was done using a Zeiss Gemini SEM 450. Viscosity was measured with an MCR Rheometer 102. A parallel plate setup with 50 mm was used. Shear rates ranged from 10 to 300 s⁻¹. Measurements were taken at 10, 20, 30, and 40°C. Thermal analysis used DSC 1Star from Mettler Toledo. The temperature range was from -120 to 90°C. The cooling rate was 1°C per minute. A 5-minute isotherm was applied at -120°C. The heating rate was 1°C per minute. Samples were equilibrated at 30°C for 30 minutes. TGA was carried out using Mettler Toledo TGA/DSC-1. Conductivity was measured with EIS using a dip probe cell. The cell factor was 1.04 cm⁻¹. The frequency range was 1 Hz to 200 kHz. The amplitude was 25 mV. Samples were degassed with nitrogen flux. Measurements were done under N2 flux from 5 to 70°C. Electrode slurries used a weight ratio of 8:1:1. Anhydrous N-Methyl-2-Pyrrolidone was used as solvent. Active material loads were 2.4, 2.7, and 1.7 mg cm⁻² for Li, Na, and K cells. Benchmark cells used 1.0 M LiPF6 in EC/DMC. Benchmark cells used 1 M NaClO4 in PC/FEC. Benchmark cells used 0.8 M KPF6 in EC/DEC. NASICON electrodes for aqueous electrolytes used dip-coating. The active material load was 6 mg cm⁻². ESW was estimated in flooded three-electrode cells. Glassy carbon was used as the working electrode. Platinum mesh was used as the counter electrode. Double junction SCE was used as the reference electrode. GCPL technique was used at different current rates. Measurements started with 10 cycles at 0.1 C. The current increased to 0.5, 1, 5, and 10 C. The current was reduced to 0.1 C for the last 10 cycles. 1C corresponds to 136 mA g⁻¹. EIS measurements were conducted from 20 to 70°C. The frequency range was 1 kHz to 100 kHz. The sinusoidal voltage was 50 mV. Impedance measurements were carried out in a Faraday cage.

Procedures And Architectures
The CLTP synthesis used a glucose carbon precursor. The LTP synthesis omitted glucose. The XRD patterns showed phase purity without secondary phases. The crystal structure is rhombohedral NASICON type (R-3c). The peak positions were the same in both samples. The carbon content did not affect the crystal structure. The ionic conductivity followed VTF behavior. The ionic conductivity decreased with increasing concentration. The viscosity followed Arrhenius behavior. The viscosity increased with concentration. The viscosity trend did not vary linearly. The acetate salts are structure-making salts. None of the samples showed a decrease in viscosity. The samples behaved like Newtonian fluids. The molar conductivities were plotted against fluidity. The electrolytes were classified as quasi-ideal. The most concentrated solution followed Kohlrausch's law. The molar conductivity at infinite dilution was 52.90 ohm⁻¹ cm² mol⁻¹. The Kohlrausch law calls for complete salt dissociation. The LSV profiles were measured vs SHE. A threshold of 0.1 mA cm⁻² was used for decomposition potentials. The procedure may lead to overestimated decomposition limits. The procedure is highly reproducible. The cathodic stability increased with concentration. The anodic ESW expansion was not as significant. The impedance spectra showed a depressed semicircle. The straight line relates to the Warburg element. The Arrhenius plot showed low activation energy. The low activation energy proved good interfacial kinetics. The diffusion coefficient was calculated via a formula. The number of mobile ions was evaluated to be 1.7. The concentration of mobile ions was 12930 mol m⁻³. The diffusion coefficient at room temperature was around 10⁻¹³ cm² s⁻¹. The aqueous electrolyte improved ion diffusion. The low activation energy for diffusion was 0.48 eV.

Key Results
The glass transition temperature increased with salt concentration. The Tg values are reported in Table 2. The Tg transition reflects the shift from salt-in-water to water-in-salt. The 1N20K and 2.5N20K samples showed no cold crystallization. The 5N20K and 7N20K samples showed cold crystallization events. The melting endotherms were recorded for both samples.
